hops.afterHeading: The worked cohort, column by column
hops.title: Edmond Halley prices annuities with a life table
hops.text: In 1693 the English government was selling life annuities at one rate for every age: 14% of the price paid back each year for life, which Halley called seven years' purchase. The same year, astronomer Edmond Halley worked from five years of Breslau birth and burial records, averaging 1,238 births a year, and estimated how many were living at each age. Pricing annuities from it at 6% interest, he valued one on a child of about ten at 13.44 years' purchase, nearly twice the government's rate, and one on a seventy-year-old at only 5.32. A baby in its first year, when deaths ran highest, came to 10.28.

sources.citation: Halley E. (1693), Philosophical Transactions 17:596-610, transcription at the University of York history of statistics pages.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A wooden desk with a brass telescope, a closed ledger, a quill pen, a tall stack of gold coins beside a toy horse and a short stack beside a walking cane.
image.caption: One flat price ignored survival: Halley valued a child's annuity at about two and a half times a seventy-year-old's.

hops.title: Did Victorians really grow old at forty?
hops.text: Life expectancy at birth in England and Wales in 1841 was 40.2 years for boys and 42.2 for girls, which makes it sound as if Victorians went grey and frail at forty. They did not. In the 1840s about 15% of babies died before their first birthday, and every one of those short lives went into the average. A boy who simply made it to his first birthday in 1841 could expect to reach 47.7, about seven and a half years more than a newborn. A man who reached 65 could expect another 10.9 years, and a woman another 11.5.

sources.citation: UK Office for National Statistics, How has life expectancy changed over time? (Sept. 9, 2015).
UK Office for National Statistics, expected age reached by age, England and Wales males, 1841 to 2011 (chart data, 2015).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An elderly couple in 19th-century clothing sitting on a garden bench, feeding sparrows.
image.caption: Infant deaths dragged 1841 life expectancy at birth down; people who reached 65 could expect their mid-seventies.

hops.afterHeading: Where the numbers come from, and what they miss
hops.title: When the identification band changes the survival rate
hops.text: Many penguin studies follow birds by fitting a metal band around one flipper, then noting who comes back. In a ten-year study of free-ranging king penguins, researchers compared banded birds with unbanded ones. Over the decade, apparent survival at the colony was 16 percentage points lower for the banded birds, and they fledged 41% fewer chicks. Even after ten years they still arrived later to breed and made longer foraging trips, so they never got used to the band. The tag meant to measure survival was lowering it. So marked birds can give a misleading picture of the unbanded birds they are meant to stand for.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two king penguins swimming underwater; an unbanded penguin glides ahead of one wearing a metal flipper band.
image.caption: Metal flipper bands lowered king penguin survival and chick output, skewing the very estimates they were meant to make.
